text: The town of Harrowgate sits at the mouth of a narrow river, where the grey water meets the sea in a long line of foam. For three hundred years its people have made their living from the tide: fishermen setting out before dawn, net makers mending twine in the lamplight, and merchants who weighed the catch on brass scales before it was packed in salt and sent inland by cart. In the autumn the harbour fills with boats seeking shelter from the storms that roll in from the west, and the cafes along the quay serve hot soup to sailors who have not slept in two days. The old lighthouse, built of local granite in the year the railway arrived, still turns its lamp every night, though nobody remembers the last time a ship depended on it. Children learn to swim in the shallow bay each summer, and their grandparents sit on the benches by the sea wall and tell stories about the great flood, the winter the harbour froze solid, and the captain who sailed to the far south and returned with a parrot that could recite a whole verse of a hymn. Visitors often say the place feels untouched by time, but the residents know better. Every year a few more young people leave for the cities, the school has fewer pupils, and the fish are harder to find.
